blocks.html: Learning objectives

By the end of this week you will be able to:

  1. Define information security and explain the CIA triad (confidentiality, integrity, availability).
  2. Explain why the three properties trade off against each other, and what "balancing CIA" means.
  3. Describe defence in depth and the phases of an attack, and why a defender studies them.
  4. Explain the assume breach mindset and what it changes about how systems are defended.
Connection to Unit Learning Outcomes

• ULO 1:
  • ULO 2:
The week's idea: assume breach

The old question in security was "how do we keep attackers out?" The better one is "what do we do given that, sooner or later, they get in?" No single control is ever enough, so a defender learns to think in layers, watch for the intrusion, limit how far it spreads, and plan to recover. This first week sets up that mindset. Everything else in the unit hangs off it.

The breach you vote through in this week's lecture is not a one-off exercise, either: modules 2–4 are its investigation. Each week rewinds the same incident one layer deeper: how they got in, what they took, and what held.

lessons.title: Lab: Environment setup and access control

blocks.html: This week's lab
The hands-on labs run in a provided, container-based environment. You do not need to know Docker: one command starts everything, and you drive the lab with plain commands.
Getting the lab environment

1. Install Docker Desktop following the environment setup guide (it covers Windows, macOS and Linux, and what to do when it won't install).
  2. Download the labs: assume-breach-labs ZIP; unzip it anywhere.
  3. Start the lab: in the unzipped folder, run ./start.sh (Windows: double-click start.bat) and choose module 01: Access control.
  4. The steps: follow the Module 01: Access control lab guide from top to bottom; everything the lab asks of you is in there.

This week you complete two short modules:

  1. Environment setup: get the lab running and confirm it works.
  2. Access control. Meet users, groups, and permissions: the first, most basic security control, and a direct example of confidentiality and least privilege from the reading.

Can't run it on your own machine? The labs site explains the browser-based option (no install required). Follow the lab guide for each module; ask your tutor if you get stuck.
Your Lab Passport

In the last few minutes of the lab, make your first Lab Passport entry: a short, handwritten reflection, handed in as you leave. This is Assessment 1; there is no separate report; the collected passport is the assessment. This week's prompt:

What does "thinking like a defender" mean to you after today, and why would a business care?

Write 4–6 sentences, in your own words. Best 8 of 10 weekly entries count.
Learning objectives

By the end of this week you will be able to:

  1. Distinguish a design flaw from an implementation flaw, and explain what attack surface is and why a defender shrinks it.
  2. Explain what CVE and CWE are, how responsible disclosure works, and why a zero-day is dangerous.
  3. Classify the main families of malware (virus, worm, trojan, RAT, ransomware, rootkit, botnet) by how they spread and survive.
  4. Trace how a real breach chains several flaws together, and name the ordinary controls that would have broken the chain.
Connection to Unit Learning Outcomes

• ULO 2:
  • ULO 3:
The week's idea: most attacks walk through a door someone left open

Very few attacks break the maths. They exploit a mistake in the software, or a person willing to run something they shouldn't. Once you see those two doors, "gaining access" stops being magic and becomes a list of things a defender can close: reduce the attack surface, patch the flaws, limit what code can run, and never trust one control to hold. That is assume breach applied to software.

This is also the first rewind of Module 1's First Breach: the investigation opens with how did they get in? The lab has you take the attacker's own first step to find out.

Lecture (2 h) Malware line-up, then trace a real breach chain and vote the control that breaks each link lecture-slides

Lab Passport A short handwritten reflection, handed in at the end of the lab in the lab

This week's lab

Lab: Port scanning and enumeration. You take the attacker's first practical step, reconnaissance, against a small internal lab network, and discover which hosts and services are reachable. That list of open ports is the attack surface from the reading, made concrete. All targets are inside the provided lab; you never scan the real internet. Labs site: .
Looking ahead
Next week: Authentication & Access: passwords, why they fail, and how attackers crack them.
This week's lab
The hands-on labs run in a provided, container-based environment. You do not need to know Docker: one command starts everything, and you drive the lab with plain commands.
Getting this week's lab

1. First time only: install Docker Desktop (see the environment setup guide), then download the labs, assume-breach-labs ZIP, and unzip it anywhere.
  2. Start the lab: in the unzipped folder, run ./start.sh (Windows: double-click start.bat) and choose module 02: Port scanning & enumeration.
  3. The steps: follow the Module 02: Port scanning & enumeration lab guide from top to bottom; everything the lab asks of you is in there.

This week you take the attacker's first practical step, reconnaissance, against a small internal lab network. Using Nmap you discover which hosts are alive, which ports are open, and which services are listening. That list of open ports is exactly the attack surface from the reading, seen from the outside. You will notice how a service that no one turned off is a door left open.

All targets are inside the provided lab network. You never scan the real internet or any system you do not own. Scanning systems without permission is unlawful, and it is the line between what you are learning and what an attacker does.

Can't run it on your own machine? The labs site explains the browser-based option (GitHub Codespaces, no install required). Follow the lab guide for the module; ask your tutor if you get stuck.
Your Lab Passport

In the last few minutes of the lab, make your Lab Passport entry: a short, handwritten reflection, handed in as you leave. This is Assessment 1; there is no separate report; the collected passport is the assessment. This week's prompt:

You scanned a network and saw its open ports. Pick one service you found and argue, as a defender, whether it should be open at all, and how you would decide.

Write 4–6 sentences, in your own words. Best 8 of 10 weekly entries count.
Learning objectives

By the end of this week you will be able to:

  1. Distinguish identification, authentication, and authorisation, and explain least privilege in those terms.
  2. Explain the three factors of authentication and what multi-factor authentication does and does not add.
  3. Explain why a good system stores a salted hash of a password, never the password itself.
  4. Analyse password attacks (dictionary, brute-force, rainbow tables) and name the defence that beats each.
Connection to Unit Learning Outcomes

• ULO 1:
  • ULO 3:
The week's idea: a password isn't stored as a password

Every system starts with one question: who are you, and are you allowed to be here? The secret behind the answer is never kept as-is: it is hashed, and salted, so that stealing the database does not hand over everyone's password. Understanding what is actually stored, and how attackers attack it, is the whole of this week. And as always, the maths is rarely the weakest link; the people and the plumbing around it are.

The First Breach rewind continues: we know how they got in (Module 2); this week asks what did they take? The stolen login database in the lecture is that company's own, and in the lab you crack its hashes yourself.
How this week works

Part What you do Where
Before class Read Chapter 3, watch the summary, do the quiz pre-class/
Lecture (2 h) A defender adds one login control at a time; the class votes whether each attack still gets through lecture-slides
Lab (1 h) Crack real password hashes and see for yourself why length and salt matter in-class/
Lab Passport A short handwritten reflection, handed in at the end of the lab in the lab
Before class

1. [ ] Read , Chapter 3: Authentication & Access**,
  2. [ ] Watch the ~10-minute narrated summary (pre-class/summary-slides)

This week's lab

Lab: Password attacks. Using John the Ripper against hashes provided in the lab, you run a dictionary attack and a brute-force attack, and see directly how quickly weak passwords fall and how much length and salting change the game. Everything is offline and self-contained. Labs site: .
Looking ahead
Next week: Cryptography, the maths behind that hash, and the one idea (Kerckhoff's principle) that organises the whole field.
This week's lab
The hands-on labs run in a provided, container-based environment. You do not need to know Docker: one command starts everything, and you drive the lab with plain commands.
Getting this week's lab

1. First time only: install Docker Desktop (setup guide on the labs site), then download the labs, assume-breach-labs ZIP, and unzip it anywhere.
  2. Start the lab: in the unzipped folder, run ./start.sh (Windows: double-click start.bat) and choose module 03: Password attacks.
  3. The steps: follow the Module 03: Password attacks lab guide from top to bottom; everything the lab asks of you is in there.

This week you attack passwords the way an attacker does: not by reversing the hash, but by guessing, hashing, and matching. Using John the Ripper against hashes provided in the lab, you run a dictionary attack and a brute-force attack, and see for yourself how fast weak passwords fall, how much length slows an attacker down, and how salt removes their shortcut. Everything is offline and self-contained.

You are cracking hashes provided inside the lab for teaching. Never attempt to crack passwords or hashes you are not explicitly authorised to test. The skill is for defenders; the authorisation is what keeps it lawful.

Can't run it on your own machine? The labs site explains the browser-based option (GitHub Codespaces, no install required). Follow the lab guide; ask your tutor if you get stuck.
Your Lab Passport

In the last few minutes of the lab, make your Lab Passport entry: a short, handwritten reflection, handed in as you leave. This is Assessment 1; there is no separate report; the collected passport is the assessment. This week's prompt:

You cracked weak password hashes today. As a defender, what would you require of your users, and of the system that stores their passwords, and what would still keep you up at night?

Write 4–6 sentences, in your own words. Best 8 of 10 weekly entries count.
Learning objectives

By the end of this week you will be able to:

  1. Explain the difference between an algorithm and a key, and state Kerckhoff's principle.
  2. Distinguish symmetric from asymmetric cryptography and say what each is good for.
  3. Explain the difference between hashing and encryption, and where digital signatures fit.
  4. Reason about why weak ciphers fail, and why real systems attack the plumbing, not the maths.
Connection to Unit Learning Outcomes

• ULO 1:
  • ULO 3:
The week's idea: the secret is the key, not the method

A good cipher is secure even when the enemy knows exactly how it works. Its strength rests entirely on the secrecy of the key, never on hiding the algorithm. That is Kerckhoff's principle, and it explains why the ciphers you should trust are the ones published and attacked by the whole world for years. You do not need the mathematics to reason about cryptography well: you need to know what each kind guarantees, what it doesn't, and where the real weaknesses lie (which, as ever, are rarely in the maths).

This is the last rewind of First Breach, and its best ending: among everything the attacker took, one properly encrypted file never gave. This week explains why: the one control that kept working after the breach, which is assume breach's whole argument in a single file.
How this week works

Part What you do Where
Before class Read Chapter 4, watch the summary, do the quiz pre-class/
Lecture (2 h) Break a weak cipher live, discover why public algorithms win, sort encrypt-vs-hash lecture-slides
Lab (1 h) Encrypt and decrypt with a real cipher and with GnuPG public keys in-class/
Lab Passport A short handwritten reflection, handed in at the end of the lab in the lab

This week's lab

Lab: Cryptography. You use a cipher tool to encrypt and decrypt messages, watch a weak cipher give up its secret, and use GnuPG to generate a key pair and exchange an encrypted message the asymmetric way. Everything runs offline in the provided environment. Labs site: .
Looking ahead

This week's lab
The hands-on labs run in a provided, container-based environment. You do not need to know Docker: one command starts everything, and you drive the lab with plain commands.
Getting this week's lab

1. First time only: install Docker Desktop (setup guide on the labs site), then download the labs, assume-breach-labs ZIP, and unzip it anywhere.
  2. Start the lab: in the unzipped folder, run ./start.sh (Windows: double-click start.bat) and choose module 04: Cryptography.
  3. The steps: follow the Module 04: Cryptography lab guide from top to bottom; everything the lab asks of you is in there.

This week you get your hands on cryptography directly. Using a cipher tool you encrypt and decrypt a message and watch a weak cipher give up its secret to simple analysis. Then, with GnuPG, you generate a public/private key pair and exchange an encrypted message the asymmetric way, seeing how someone can send you a secret using only your public key. Everything runs offline in the provided environment; there are no online key servers or web tools.

Can't run it on your own machine? The labs site explains the browser-based option (GitHub Codespaces, no install required). Follow the lab guide; ask your tutor if you get stuck.
Your Lab Passport

In the last few minutes of the lab, make your Lab Passport entry: a short, handwritten reflection, handed in as you leave. This is Assessment 1. There is no separate report; the collected passport is the assessment. This week's prompt:

Explain to a non-technical manager, in your own words, why "we wrote our own secret encryption algorithm" should worry them rather than reassure them.

Write 4–6 sentences, in your own words. Best 8 of 10 weekly entries count.
Learning objectives

By the end of this week you will be able to:

  1. Define risk as likelihood × impact, and explain why risk appetite varies between organisations.
  2. Distinguish intrinsic from acquired value, and use cost-benefit analysis to judge a control.
  3. Calculate single loss expectancy (SLE) and annual loss expectancy (ALE), and decide whether a control is worth buying.
  4. Describe the four risk treatments (avoid, mitigate, transfer, accept) and when each is the right call.
Connection to Unit Learning Outcomes

• ULO 3:
  • ULO 4:
The week's idea: you can't protect everything, so decide well

No organisation has unlimited money or time, so a defender who tries to protect everything equally protects nothing well. Risk management is the discipline of deciding, honestly and defensibly, what to protect, how much to spend, and what to leave alone. This is where security stops being a technical subject and becomes a business one, and where "assume breach" turns into a budget.
How this week works

Part What you do Where
Before class Read Chapter 5, watch the summary, do the quiz pre-class/
Lecture (2 h) Spend a fixed security budget as a team; compute what each control actually saves lecture-slides
Lab (1 h) Use an SLE/ALE calculator to size risks and judge controls with real numbers in-class/
Lab Passport A short handwritten reflection, handed in at the end of the lab in the lab
Before class

  3. [ ] Do the pre-class quiz on Blackboard (pre-class/quiz)
This week's lab

Lab: Risk (SLE/ALE). In a browser-based calculator you put numbers on real risks (single loss expectancy, annualised rate of occurrence, annual loss expectancy) and test whether a proposed control actually saves money. It is the quantitative backbone of the Case Study you are about to begin. Labs site: .
Looking ahead
Next week: Incident & Disaster Planning, what you do when a risk you accepted or mitigated happens anyway. This is also where the Case Study launches.
This week's lab

The hands-on labs run in a provided, container-based environment. You do not need to know Docker: one command starts everything. This week's lab is browser-based: the environment serves a small web page to your browser, and there is no command line to learn.
Getting this week's lab

1. First time only: install Docker Desktop (setup guide on the labs site), then download the labs, assume-breach-labs ZIP, and unzip it anywhere.
  2. Start the lab: in the unzipped folder, run ./start.sh (Windows: double-click start.bat) and choose module 05: Risk management.
  3. The steps: follow the Module 05: Risk management lab guide from top to bottom; everything the lab asks of you is in there.

This week you put real numbers on risk. Using an SLE/ALE calculator you work through several scenarios: estimate the single loss expectancy, choose an annualised rate of occurrence, and read off the annual loss expectancy. Then you test a proposed control: does the reduction in ALE actually beat what the control costs? You will find, as in the lecture, that the answer is sometimes no. This is the exact reasoning the Case Study runs on, so treat the lab as a warm-up for it.

Can't run it on your own machine? The labs site explains the browser-based option (GitHub Codespaces, no install required). Follow the lab guide; ask your tutor if you get stuck.
Your Lab Passport

In the last few minutes of the lab, make your Lab Passport entry: a short, handwritten reflection, handed in as you leave. This is Assessment 1; there is no separate report; the collected passport is the assessment. This week's prompt:

From today's scenarios, pick one control you decided not to buy. Justify that decision as a defender, using cost versus the reduction in annual loss, not gut feeling.

Write 4–6 sentences, in your own words. Best 8 of 10 weekly entries count.
Learning objectives

By the end of this week you will be able to:

  1. Distinguish incident response, business continuity, and disaster recovery, and give an example of each.
  2. Explain RTO and RPO and why the RPO dictates the backup schedule.
  3. Describe a good incident-response lifecycle (detect → respond → recover → learn) and the role of pre-decided roles and communication.
  4. Explain the 3-2-1 backup rule, alternate sites, breach-notification clocks, and why an untested plan is only a hope.
Connection to Unit Learning Outcomes

• ULO 3:
  • ULO 4:
The week's idea: decide what you'll do *before* the worst day

This is the week assume breach stops being a slogan and becomes a plan. Prevention has a ceiling; past it, the only thing that helps is preparation to respond. The organisations that survive a breach are the ones that decided in advance what they would do, calmly, not at 3 a.m. during the worst day of the company's year. Planning for failure is the most practical form of optimism there is.

And the worst day has an address. Remember Bassendean Medical Supplies, the shop you defended in First Breach? Their customer list includes an allied-health provider called Rivergum Health: three clinics, 48,000 patient files, two IT staff. The supplier's breach was November. This week, at 6 a.m. on a Saturday, it is Rivergum's turn, and you are the one on call.

There is no container lab this week. Instead the hour launches Assessment 2, the **** Essential Eight gap analysis (35%), and gives you a catch-up slot for any earlier lab you did not finish.

1. Form your team

Get into your assessment teams. Your tutor will confirm sizes and record membership. The individual viva later means everyone must genuinely understand the team's work, so choose to contribute from day one.

2. Meet the brief

You will receive the Case Study brief and the * materials on the LMS: the maturity model, the process guide, and the report template. Your job across the coming weeks is to assess a real target (*) against the Essential Eight controls, identify the gaps, and recommend improvements to a senior stakeholder. Today, read the brief together and agree who does what.

3. Plan your approach

Sketch a plan: which controls each member will assess, how you will gather evidence, and when you will meet. The risk reasoning from last week (SLE/ALE, the four treatments) is the backbone of your recommendations.

4. Catch up (if needed)

If a Docker lab from Weeks 1–6 did not finish on your machine, use this time and your tutor to complete it. Labs site: .
Optional: run the incident live
If your tutor has , its Disaster Recovery** module turns today's tabletop into a timed game against the 72-hour clock. →
Your Lab Passport

In the last few minutes, make your Lab Passport entry: a short, handwritten reflection, handed in as you leave. This is Assessment 1: there is no separate report; the collected passport is the assessment. This week's prompt:

After today's incident tabletop, name the one decision your team most needs to make before a real breach, and explain why deciding it in advance matters.

Write 4–6 sentences, in your own words. Best 8 of 10 weekly entries count.
Learning objectives

By the end of this week you will be able to:

  1. Explain how scanning and sniffing work and what each reveals about a network.
  2. Describe what a packet capture shows, and why unencrypted traffic is so dangerous.
  3. Describe spoofing and man-in-the-middle attacks, and why a local attacker is special.
  4. Explain how encryption in transit, segmentation, and monitoring turn an open wire back into a private one.
Connection to Unit Learning Outcomes

• ULO 1:
  • ULO 3:
The week's idea: everything you send crosses wires you don't control

On a network, an attacker often doesn't need to break into your machine to learn your secrets. They only have to listen. A surprising amount of traffic gives itself away in plain text, including usernames and passwords typed in the clear. This week is about how attackers map and eavesdrop on networks, and the single change (encryption in transit) that neutralises passive listening.
How this week works

Part What you do Where

This week's lab

Lab: Packet capture & analysis. Using Wireshark in the browser, you open real teaching captures and reassemble the conversations crossing the wire, including a login sent in the clear. Then you compare it with encrypted traffic and see the difference for yourself. All captures are provided in the lab. Labs site: .
Looking ahead
Next week: VPN & Firewalls, the two classic defences that decide what traffic is allowed and protect what's in motion.
This week's lab

The hands-on labs run in a provided, container-based environment. You do not need to know Docker: one command starts everything. This week's tool, Wireshark, runs in your browser, so there is nothing to install.
Getting this week's lab

1. First time only: install Docker Desktop (setup guide on the labs site), then download the labs, assume-breach-labs ZIP, and unzip it anywhere.
  2. Start the lab: in the unzipped folder, run ./start.sh (Windows: double-click start.bat) and choose module 06: Packet capture & analysis (lab modules are numbered by topic, so the number differs from our module).
  3. The steps: follow the Module 06: Packet capture & analysis lab guide from top to bottom; everything the lab asks of you is in there.

This week you read the wire. You open real teaching packet captures and reassemble the conversations crossing the network, following a stream until a login sent over an old, unencrypted protocol gives up its username and password in plain text. Then you open an encrypted capture and see the same kind of traffic reduced to unreadable ciphertext. The contrast is the whole lesson: sniffing shows everything that isn't encrypted.

All captures are provided inside the lab. Capturing traffic on networks you are not authorised to monitor is unlawful. The skill is for defenders auditing their own systems.

Can't run it on your own machine? The labs site explains the browser-based option (GitHub Codespaces, no install required). Follow the lab guide; ask your tutor if you get stuck.
Your Lab Passport

In the last few minutes of the lab, make your Lab Passport entry: a short, handwritten reflection, handed in as you leave. This is Assessment 1. There is no separate report; the collected passport is the assessment. This week's prompt:

You watched a plaintext password appear in a capture. Explain to a friend who uses public Wi-Fi what they should change about how they browse, and why, in terms of what an eavesdropper can and cannot see.

Write 4–6 sentences, in your own words. Best 8 of 10 weekly entries count.
Learning objectives

By the end of this week you will be able to:

  1. Explain what a firewall does and distinguish packet-filtering, stateful, and application-layer firewalls.
  2. Reason about firewall rules: default-deny vs default-allow, why order matters, and why over-broad rules are dangerous.
  3. Explain what a VPN provides (confidentiality and integrity over an untrusted network) and, crucially, what it does not.
  4. Describe defence in depth in a network context: firewall, VPN, segmentation, and monitoring together.
Connection to Unit Learning Outcomes

• ULO 1:
  • ULO 3:
The week's idea: the tool is easy, the rule is hard

A firewall decides what traffic to let through; a VPN protects traffic in transit. Both are everyday tools and both are widely misunderstood. A firewall doesn't understand intent: it applies your policy literally, so its security is the quality of the thinking in its rules. Writing a good rule is harder than it sounds, and that difficulty is the lesson.
How this week works

Part What you do Where
Before class Read Chapter 8, watch the summary, do the quiz pre-class/
Lecture (2 h) Write a firewall policy as a class and watch one misordered rule open a hole lecture-slides
Lab (1 h) Build and test firewall rules between two zones, and see default-deny in action in-class/
Lab Passport A short handwritten reflection, handed in at the end of the lab in the lab

This week's lab

Lab: Firewalls. You work with a firewall between an inside network it protects and an outside it distrusts, writing and testing rules to allow what should pass and block the rest. You will see how default-deny fails safe, how rule order changes the outcome, and how one over-broad line opens a hole. Labs site: .
Looking ahead
Next week: Web Security & Data Protection, the most-attacked surface of all, and the law that governs the data behind it.
This week's lab
The hands-on labs run in a provided, container-based environment. You do not need to know Docker: one command starts everything, and you drive the lab with plain commands.
Getting this week's lab

1. First time only: install Docker Desktop (setup guide on the labs site), then download the labs, assume-breach-labs ZIP, and unzip it anywhere.
  2. Start the lab: in the unzipped folder, run ./start.sh (Windows: double-click start.bat) and choose module 07: Firewalls (lab modules are numbered by topic, so the number differs from our module).
  3. The steps: follow the Module 07: Firewalls lab guide from top to bottom; everything the lab asks of you is in there.

This week you work with a firewall between two zones: an inside network it protects and an outside it distrusts. You write and test rules to allow what should pass and block the rest, and you see the lessons from the lecture become real:

  • default-deny fails safe: anything you didn't allow is blocked;
  • order matters: moving a rule up or down changes what gets through;
  • one over-broad rule quietly opens a hole.

You test each rule by trying to reach across the boundary and watching what the firewall does with your traffic.

Can't run it on your own machine? The labs site explains the browser-based option (GitHub Codespaces, no install required). Follow the lab guide; ask your tutor if you get stuck.
Your Lab Passport

In the last few minutes of the lab, make your Lab Passport entry: a short, handwritten reflection, handed in as you leave. This is Assessment 1: there is no separate report; the collected passport is the assessment. This week's prompt:

You opened a hole with a single misordered or over-broad rule. Explain why a firewall can be "on" and correctly running yet still leave a network exposed, and what that means for how you'd review a real rule set.

Write 4–6 sentences, in your own words. Best 8 of 10 weekly entries count.
Learning objectives

By the end of this week you will be able to:

  1. Explain the most common web vulnerabilities (injection/SQL injection, cross-site scripting (XSS), and session attacks) at a working level.
  2. Trace how a web attack unfolds and identify the recurring root cause: trusting input that should not be trusted.
  3. Explain core data-protection obligations (the privacy principles and mandatory breach notification) using the APPs/NDB and GDPR as examples.
  4. Explain why a web vulnerability is, in the same instant, a privacy incident.
Connection to Unit Learning Outcomes

• ULO 2:
  • ULO 4:
The week's idea: a web flaw is a privacy incident

The web is where most of us are attacked, because it's where most of us are; it is the single largest attack surface most organisations have. Behind every web app is data someone is legally obliged to protect. So a single injection or XSS flaw that spills a customer database is a technical failure and a legal event at the same moment: it starts the breach-notification clock and exposes the organisation to real penalty. The vulnerability and the consequence are two faces of one event.

  • bypass a login with an injection;
  • fire a cross-site script and watch it run in the page;
  • see how a hijacked session lets someone act as another user.

Each is the concrete version of a flaw from the reading, and each traces back to the same root cause: input that should not have been trusted.

You attack your own provided instance of Juice Shop, running locally in the lab. Never use these techniques against any website you are not explicitly authorised to test. The app is built for practice; the authorisation is what keeps it lawful.

You exploited a web flaw that could spill customer data. Explain why fixing the bug is only half the response: what does the organisation now owe the people whose data was exposed, and why?

Learning objectives

By the end of this week you will be able to:

  1. Explain what a botnet is, why its value is aggregate, and how it is built and monetised.
  2. Describe the cybercrime economy, the division of labour, and why specialisation makes attacks so hard to stop.
  3. Reconstruct a timeline from forensic traces (logs, timestamps, email headers, document metadata).
  4. Explain chain of custody and why attribution is spoken of in terms of confidence, not certainty.
Connection to Unit Learning Outcomes

The week's idea: modern attacks are a business

The lone hacker in a hoodie is decades out of date. Serious cybercrime is organised, professional, and about money: an economy with suppliers, specialists, and marketplaces. Once you see it as an economy you stop asking "who would do this?" and start asking "who profits, and how do I make it unprofitable?" And when an attack succeeds, the work shifts to forensics: following the money and the evidence back to its source, without destroying the evidence on the way.

This week's lab
The hands-on labs run in a provided, container-based environment. You do not need to know Docker: one command starts everything, and you drive the lab with plain commands.
Getting this week's lab

1. First time only: install Docker Desktop (setup guide on the labs site), then download the labs, assume-breach-labs ZIP, and unzip it anywhere.
  2. Start the lab: in the unzipped folder, run ./start.sh (Windows: double-click start.bat) and choose module 08: Digital forensics (lab modules are numbered by topic, so the number differs from our module).
  3. The steps: follow the Module 08: Digital forensics lab guide from top to bottom; everything the lab asks of you is in there.

This week you follow the trail. Using two offline tools you:

  • analyse email headers to trace a message's real path and origin, seeing through an attempt to hide where it came from; and
  • use stylometry (authorship analysis) to reason about who wrote a document from the way it is written.

From fragments like these an investigator builds a defensible timeline. As you work, keep the lecture's warning in mind: the moment you handle evidence carelessly, you can no longer prove it wasn't altered.

Can't run it on your own machine? The labs site explains the browser-based option (GitHub Codespaces, no install required). Follow the lab guide; ask your tutor if you get stuck.
Your Lab Passport: final entry

In the last few minutes of the lab, make your final entry: a short, handwritten reflection. This week's prompt:

You traced a message to its source but had to be careful how you handled the evidence. Explain why an investigator can be sure who did something and still be unable to prove it, and what that means for how evidence must be handled.

Write 4–6 sentences, in your own words.
Learning objectives

By the end of this week you will be able to:

  1. Explain why the human is so often the weakest link, and why "blame the user" is the wrong response.
  2. Describe social engineering and phishing, and the defences that actually work (and why training alone is the weakest).
  3. Explain why non-technical people click through warnings like a certificate error, and why that is a design failure.
  4. Discuss emerging trends, especially AI's double role as a tool for both attackers and defenders.
Connection to Unit Learning Outcomes

• ULO 2:
  • ULO 3:
The week's idea: you can't patch a person, so design for the mistake

Every week so far has been, at heart, about machines. But security fails more often through people. The most sophisticated defences can be undone by one click, one helpful password reset, one approved urgent transfer. The professional response is not to demand perfect users; it is to assume someone will be fooled and build so the organisation survives it. That single shift, from "make users perfect" to "make mistakes survivable", is the difference between security that works and security that just apportions blame.

Getting this week's lab

  2. Start the lab: in the unzipped folder, run ./start.sh (Windows: double-click start.bat) and choose module 09: Human factors (lab modules are numbered by topic, so the number differs from our module).
  3. The steps: follow the Module 09: Human factors lab guide from top to bottom; everything the lab asks of you is in there.

This week has two parts, both self-hosted so nothing depends on an outside website:

  • a security-awareness challenge: a short quiz that tests whether you can tell a legitimate message or site from a manipulative one; and
  • a set of sites with deliberately broken certificates (expired, self-signed, wrong name), so you see the real browser warnings most people click straight past. You will learn to read what each warning actually means and why it might be the only thing standing between a user and a man-in-the-middle attacker.

The point is not to memorise the warnings, but to feel how easily a busy person dismisses them, and to design, as a defender, so that a moment of inattention is not catastrophic.

By the end of this week you will be able to:

  1. Describe the security lifecycle loop (design → harden → detect → respond → recover → investigate → audit & learn) and place every unit topic on it.
  2. Explain why assume breach is what makes the loop turn, and why it is not defeatism.
  3. Connect the unit's concepts across chapters into a single, coherent whole for the exam.

The week's idea: security has no finish line, by design

You do not secure a system the way you paint a fence: once, and it's done. CIA pulls against itself, controls fail, people slip, threats evolve. So security is a cycle you keep turning, not a state you reach. This week we join every topic in the unit into one loop and play it end to end. That shape, and the discipline to keep it turning honestly, is the single most important thing to carry out of a first course in defensive security.

blocks.html: This week: no Docker lab, the capstone

There is no container lab this week. The hour is a capstone: play the security lifecycle end to end, and finalise your Case Study.

1. Play **, in groups

** threads the whole unit into one game: design a network, harden it, detect and respond to a breach, recover from the disaster, and investigate what happened. Every module you have done maps onto a stage of the campaign, under time and budget pressure, which is where the real judgement lives.

There isn't time to play the full campaign in one hour, so we split into groups and each group plays a different stage as a standalone module:

Group Stage (standalone module) Draws on
A Design / Network Building: segment the network, place perimeter controls Modules 07–08
B Harden: shrink the attack surface with Essential Eight-style controls Modules 03–05
C Detect & Respond: run the incident-response loop against a live breach Modules 06–07
D Recover: bring the business back (backups, DR) from the disaster Module 06
E Investigate / Forensics: reconstruct and attribute what happened Module 10

Each group plays its module, then reports back in a few minutes: what the stage taught them, and where it hands off to the next. Stitched together, the room has replayed the whole lifecycle, the same arc as the full campaign, in the time available.

Use time this week to finalise your team's * gap-analysis report, confirm each member's *individual evidence of learning, and prepare for the viva. Remember every member must be able to explain the whole submission.

3. Prepare for the exam

The Final Examination (50%) follows in the examination period and focuses on applying concepts and interpreting real security artefacts. The best revision aid is Chapter 12 and the lifecycle loop from today's lecture: for each stage, be able to name the controls, the trade-offs, and how a real artefact (a firewall rule set, a packet capture, an SLE/ALE calculation, an email header) would be read.
